title: The First Cut Is the Deepest

meta.title: Who originally recorded "The First Cut Is the Deepest"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Rod Stewart. P. P. Arnold cut it first, released 21 April 1967 on Immediate Records. Cat Stevens wrote it; Stewart's hit came ten years on.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'The First Cut Is the Deepest'?
meta.ogDescription: P. P. Arnold released the first version on Immediate Records on 21 April 1967. Cat Stevens wrote it. Rod Stewart's famous 1977 single is a cover.

answer.label: Not a Rod Stewart original — a 1967 P. P. Arnold single on Immediate
answer.originalArtistDates: b. 1946 · American soul singer, Los Angeles born, London based
answer.sourceLine: Rod Stewart’s reading is so completely his own that most listeners file the song under his name. It is a cover. The first release belongs to P. P. Arnold, the American soul singer who arrived in England with the Ike & Tina Turner Revue and stayed — her single came out on Immediate Records on 21 April 1967 ↗, catalogue IM 047. It was written by Cat Stevens, who handed it over before he had made a name as a singer and did not issue his own recording until his album New Masters in December of that same year. Arnold’s record was no obscurity either: it reached No. 18 on the UK singles chart.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Immediate Records
original.released: Issued as a 7-inch A-side on Immediate Records, catalogue IM 047, on 21 April 1967, backed with “Speak to Me.” It was later gathered onto Arnold’s album The First Lady of Immediate.
original.charted: Reached No. 18 on the UK Singles Chart — a genuine hit at the time, not a lost curio.
original.cover: Rod Stewart recorded it for A Night on the Town (1976) and released it as a single in 1977 on Riva/Warner Bros. In the UK it appeared as a double A-side with “I Don’t Want to Talk About It” and spent four weeks at No. 1; in the US it reached No. 21 on the Billboard Hot 100.

trail: 21 April 1967 — P. P. Arnold’s single is released on Immediate Records, catalogue IM 047, with “Speak to Me” on the flip. It climbs to No. 18 in the UK. The release is catalogued on MusicBrainz ↗.
15 December 1967 — The writer finally releases his own version: Cat Stevens includes it on New Masters for Deram/Decca, months after Arnold’s single, per Wikipedia’s song article ↗.

April 1973 — Canadian singer Keith Hampshire takes it to No. 1 on the Canadian RPM chart on A&M, and to No. 70 on the US Billboard Hot 100 — a hit version sitting between the original and the one everyone remembers.
1977 — Rod Stewart’s single, drawn from A Night on the Town, spends four weeks at No. 1 in the UK as a double A-side and becomes, for most listeners, the definitive version.

authors.name: P. P. Arnold
authors.heading: She got there first
authors.metaLine: b. 1946, Los Angeles - American soul singer
authors.bio: Born Patricia Ann Cole in Los Angeles in 1946, she was singing as an Ikette in the Ike & Tina Turner Revue when the tour reached England in 1966. She stayed, encouraged by Mick Jagger, and signed to Immediate Records, the label run by the Rolling Stones’ manager Andrew Loog Oldham. Her single of this song, released in April 1967, reached No. 18 in the UK and remains the first version anyone put on record.

authors.name: Rod Stewart
authors.heading: The version that swallowed the song
authors.bio: Stewart cut the song for A Night on the Town in 1976 and released it as a single the following year. In the UK it went to No. 1 for four weeks as a double A-side with “I Don’t Want to Talk About It”; in the US it reached No. 21. The record is superb, and it is the reason the song is still in wide circulation — the only error in the popular account is chronological.

authors.name: Cat Stevens
authors.heading: He wrote it, then waited
authors.metaLine: b. 1948, London - British singer-songwriter, later known as Yusuf Islam
authors.bio: Stevens wrote the song early, before he was established as a performer in his own right, and let another singer release it first. His own recording appeared on New Masters in December 1967, after Arnold’s single had already charted. He has watched several different artists have hits with it since.

misattribution.heading: The record, straightened out
misattribution.intro: Almost nobody claims Rod Stewart wrote the song — the Cat Stevens credit is well known. The confusion is about whose voice reached it first, and there the popular answer is wrong.

items.why: His single topped the UK chart for four weeks and has never left the radio. For most listeners it is not a cover of anything; it is simply the song.
Released on Immediate Records, catalogue IM 047, with “Speak to Me” as the B-side. It reached No. 18 in the UK.
He wrote it and released his own version on New Masters in December 1967 — after Arnold’s single, not before it. Even Wikidata’s summary line gets this the wrong way round.
The Canadian singer took it to No. 1 in Canada on A&M years before Stewart, and reached No. 70 in the US. A hit version that has fallen out of the story entirely.

misattribution.truthLine: P. P. Arnold recorded it first, on Immediate Records, on 21 April 1967 — written by Cat Stevens, and released ahead of his own version.

context.heading: Why the cover ate the original
lead: The interesting question is not why Rod Stewart’s version is famous — it was No. 1 for four weeks and it earned that. The question is why P. P. Arnold’s is not, given that it was a top-twenty hit in its own right. Part of the answer is the label: Immediate Records was Andrew Loog Oldham’s operation, brilliant and chaotic, and it did not survive to keep her catalogue in print and in reissue the way a major would have.

The other part is that a song can only be re-introduced so many times before one voice claims it outright. By the time Stewart reached it, Cat Stevens had recorded it himself and Keith Hampshire had taken it to No. 1 in Canada. Stewart’s was the fourth notable pass and the one that stuck — so much so that Sheryl Crow’s 2003 hit was heard as a cover of a song most of her listeners already thought of as his.
detailsBody: 21 April 1967 — P. P. Arnold’s single is released on Immediate Records (IM 047), backed with “Speak to Me.” It reaches No. 18 in the UK.
15 December 1967 — Cat Stevens, the song’s writer, releases his own recording on the album New Masters for Deram/Decca.
April 1973 — Keith Hampshire’s version on A&M reaches No. 1 in Canada and No. 70 on the US Billboard Hot 100.
1976 — Rod Stewart records the song for the album A Night on the Town.
1977 — Stewart’s single reaches No. 1 in the UK for four weeks, as a double A-side with “I Don’t Want to Talk About It”, and No. 21 in the US.
22 September 2003 — Sheryl Crow’s version is released on A&M and reaches No. 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 1 on the Adult Contemporary chart.
context.pull: A top-twenty hit in 1967 is still the original, even when a bigger one arrives later.
